qc_cap_blanc_pointe_au_pic.blurb: A compact sport crag in Charlevoix, a couple of minutes from the Pointe-au-Pic casino and hotel area of La Malbaie, on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. Around 14 bolted routes climb a steep face roughly 25 m tall, with a view out over the town and river. Grades start at 5.8 but the wall leans toward the hard end: about five climbs sit in the 5.10s, a couple in the 5.11s, and six more in the 5.12s and low 5.13s. It is a short, steep, technical place best suited to climbers comfortable on 5.10 and up, and a good stop for a quick session while visiting the region.

qc_c_droite_de_l_aiguille.blurb: The right-hand side of L'Aiguille, one of the classic cliffs at Val-David in the Laurentides. This sector holds 13 routes, mostly traditional with two sport lines, spread across a wide range of difficulty: one easy low-angle line, a few in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, several in the 5.10s and 5.11s, and a couple of hard ones up to 5.13. The climbing is on steep faces, with a few multi-pitch lines and some chimneys, so it suits climbers who want a mix of trad leading and bolted faces and can place their own gear.

qc_05_hommage_radoth.blurb: A sector of L'Amphithéâtre at Saint-André-de-Kamouraska, in the Bas-Saint-Laurent. It has 13 short routes, nine of them bolted sport lines and four set up as top-ropes. The quartzite here skews difficult: one climb around 5.9, a few in the 5.10s, one 5.11, and most of the rest in the 5.12s and low 5.13s. Because the grades are stiff for this part of Quebec the wall tends to be quiet, and it gives decent cover when rain is heavy. A good option for stronger sport climbers who want to avoid the busier lines nearby.

qc_07_as_de_pique.blurb: A sector of L'Amphithéâtre at Saint-André-de-Kamouraska, in Quebec's Bas-Saint-Laurent, with 13 routes on quartzite. It splits into two parts: a main wall with sport lines, including an obvious overhanging line that is easy to spot from the approach trail, and a large detached block in front where top-rope problems are easy to rig. Grades are concentrated in the 5.10s and 5.11s, with a single 5.12. Most of the climbing is on top-rope, which makes it handy for a mixed group wanting moderate-to-hard routes without much leading.

qc_taillibert.blurb: One of two man-made urban boulders in Montreal, set near the Olympic Stadium. The block is built from granite quarried elsewhere and trucked into the city, and it opened in 2019. It carries 13 problems from V0 up to V9, with the bulk in the V2 to V5 range and a couple of harder test pieces. The face has horizontal grooves and offers overhanging, slab and technical lines. It is tall, so a rope is left on top for walking off rather than jumping. Bring your own pad; the ground below is wood chips. Good for a quick session after work.

qc_emiliana.blurb: An urban boulder in Parc des Hirondelles in Montreal, among the boulders placed there for climbers. It sits in the middle of the park behind the basketball courts, the block nearest the hammock area, and the park can be reached by car. There are 13 problems here, all on the harder side: roughly V4 to V6 for most, with one problem a notch above. Two of them, Philly Hoagie and Pain Doré, are the standout lines in the sector. Suited to climbers already comfortable on V4 who want a city bouldering session.
